prompt: A request asks for `/css/site.css` and Nginx sends the bytes of a file under its root. Which of the three kinds of answer is that?
hint: Nobody else was asked.

choices.text: A static file
choices.why: Right. The path maps to a file and the server sends it.

choices.text: A proxied answer
choices.why: Proxying means asking another program; no program was asked here.

choices.text: A cached copy kept from an earlier response
choices.why: Nothing was kept; the file was read from disk as it is.

choices.text: A redirect
choices.why: A redirect sends no file, only a new address.

prompt: The bookshop's application already speaks HTTP on port 8001. Which job is the best reason to put Nginx in front of it anyway?
hint: The work around the application is the same for every application.

choices.text: Computing a book's price from the database
choices.why: That is the one thing only the application can do.

choices.text: Holding slow connections open
choices.why: Right. That, TLS, compression and caching are the shared work a web server does well once.

choices.text: Storing the catalogue in SQLite
choices.why: The database belongs to the application, not to the web server.

choices.text: Writing the JSON for each book
choices.why: The application builds its own responses.

prompt: Which header tells you which copy of the shop answered a request?
hint: The shop names itself.

choices.text: `Server`
choices.why: `Server` names the program, ipe-shop/1.0, the same on both copies.

choices.text: `X-Served-By`
choices.why: Right. shop1 or shop2.

choices.text: `ETag`
choices.why: The ETag identifies the content, which is the same whichever copy sent it.

choices.text: `Host`
choices.why: `Host` is a request header, sent by the client.

prompt: Which way of building the course's server does lesson 1 recommend?
hint: One command creates it on any of the three desktop systems.

choices.text: A rented cloud server
choices.why: Named but not recommended: it is on the internet before lesson 4 hardens it.

choices.text: A Docker container
choices.why: The lessons lean on systemctl and services started at boot, which a plain container lacks.

choices.text: A Multipass virtual machine
choices.why: Right. Ubuntu 24.04 in a VM, on Windows, macOS or Linux.

choices.text: Installing the servers directly on your own laptop's system
choices.why: Then a broken lesson breaks your computer, and you cannot throw it away and rebuild it.

prompt: Right after `lab.sh install`, `systemctl is-active nginx apache2 caddy` prints `inactive` three times. Why?
hint: Three servers, one port 80.

choices.text: The installation failed for all three of them
choices.why: They are installed; `apt-cache policy` shows the versions.

choices.text: The install script stopped them
choices.why: Right. Ubuntu starts each one on install, and they would race for the port.

choices.text: Ubuntu never starts a server it installs
choices.why: It does, which is exactly why the script stops them.

choices.text: They need a reboot before they can run
choices.why: `systemctl enable --now` starts one without any reboot.

prompt: Why do the course's names end in `.example`?
hint: Think about who could ever own such a name.

choices.text: It is the cheapest top-level domain anyone can register
choices.why: Nobody can register it at all.

choices.text: Browsers trust it without a certificate
choices.why: No such exception exists; it does not even resolve outside the machine.

choices.text: It is reserved and never exists on the internet
choices.why: Right. RFC 2606 reserves it for exactly this.

choices.text: Nginx refuses names outside it
choices.why: Nginx serves any name a server_name lists.

prompt: `apt-get` says it could not get the lock, a minute after the machine booted. What should you do?
hint: Somebody else is installing.

choices.text: Delete the lock file so apt can continue
choices.why: That is how a package database gets corrupted while the other program is still writing.

choices.text: Reinstall Ubuntu from scratch
choices.why: Nothing is broken; another program is busy.

choices.text: Wait for Ubuntu's updates, then retry
choices.why: Right. Only one program may install at a time.

choices.text: Run the same command with `--force`
choices.why: There is no such escape, and forcing would collide with the running install.

prompt: A server will not start. Where does lesson 1 tell you to look first?
hint: Ask systemd before guessing.

choices.text: The last lines of `journalctl -u` for that service
choices.why: Right. They name the reason almost every time.

choices.text: The browser's developer tools
choices.why: The browser sees no server at all; the reason is on the machine.

choices.text: `/etc/hosts`
choices.why: Names matter for reaching a site, not for a service starting.

choices.text: A search engine
choices.why: The machine already printed the reason; read it first.

prompt: `systemctl status nginx` lists five nginx processes on a four-processor machine. What is the fifth?
hint: One of them runs as root.

choices.text: A spare worker for overload
choices.why: There is no spare; `worker_processes auto` made one per processor.

choices.text: The master process
choices.why: Right. The four workers do the serving.

choices.text: The cache manager process
choices.why: That process appears only once a proxy cache is configured, in lesson 5.

choices.text: A copy of curl
choices.why: Every process listed is nginx.

prompt: How do you switch off a site on Ubuntu's Nginx without losing its configuration?
hint: Two directories, and one holds links.

choices.text: Delete its file in `sites-available`
choices.why: That deletes the configuration itself.

choices.text: Comment out the `include` line in nginx.conf
choices.why: That switches off every site at once.

choices.text: Stop Nginx with `systemctl stop nginx`
choices.why: That stops every site, and the next start brings it back.

choices.text: Delete its link, then reload
choices.why: Right. The file in `sites-available` stays.

prompt: `curl http://localhost/css/site.css` answers 404 while `curl -H 'Host: www.ipelivros.example' http://localhost/css/site.css` answers 200. Same machine, same port. What decided the difference?
hint: Which server block did each request reach?

choices.text: The Host header: `localhost` matched no server_name and went to the default site, whose root has no such file
choices.why: Right. The site is chosen by name, not by address.

choices.text: The address 127.0.0.1 is refused
choices.why: Both requests went to 127.0.0.1; one got 200.

choices.text: The file is only readable by name
choices.why: Files have no idea which name was asked for.

choices.text: A cache answered the second one
choices.why: No cache is configured in lesson 1.

prompt: Nginx's `ETag` for site.css was `"6a96cc50-ed"`. The part after the dash is the file's size in hexadecimal. What is the size in bytes?
hint: `Content-Length` said it too.

prompt: Before every reload of Nginx, run `nginx ___` to test the configuration.
hint: A one-letter flag.

prompt: Apache will not start and the journal says `(98)Address already in use: AH00072: make_sock: could not bind to address 0.0.0.0:80`. What does it mean?
hint: A port belongs to one program at a time.

choices.text: Apache's configuration has a typo in it
choices.why: A typo fails `configtest`; this one is about a socket.

choices.text: Nginx already holds port 80
choices.why: Right. Use another port, or put one server in front of the other.

choices.text: The machine has no network
choices.why: Listening on a local port needs no outside network.

choices.text: The ServerName is missing
choices.why: That is AH00558, a warning that appears on every start.

prompt: Match each Apache piece to its Nginx counterpart.
hint: Same ideas, different words.

prompt: Why did an old Apache running `mod_php` run out of memory with a few hundred visitors?
hint: Which MPM does mod_php force?

choices.text: PHP leaks memory on every request
choices.why: The cost described is structural, not a leak.

choices.text: `.htaccess` files are cached in memory
choices.why: They are read per request, not kept; and they cost time, not this memory.

choices.text: It needs `prefork`, one whole process per connection
choices.why: Right. mod_php does not tolerate threads.

choices.text: The event MPM keeps every idle connection in its own thread
choices.why: event does the opposite: a listener thread watches idle connections.

prompt: On a server you control, what is the cost of allowing `.htaccess` files?
hint: When are they read?

choices.text: Every request searches each directory for one
choices.why: Right. That is why Ubuntu sets AllowOverride None.

choices.text: Apache stops reading the main configuration file
choices.why: Both are read; .htaccess adds to it per directory.

choices.text: They force Apache to switch to the prefork MPM
choices.why: The MPM is a module choice, unrelated to .htaccess.

choices.text: They disable TLS
choices.why: Nothing like that.

prompt: Why does the bookshop's Caddyfile write `http://` in front of each address?
hint: What does Caddy do by default for a site with a domain name?

choices.text: Caddy only serves plain HTTP on port 8081
choices.why: Caddy serves HTTPS on any port; the prefix switches it off.

choices.text: To turn off automatic HTTPS, since no certificate authority could check a .example name
choices.why: Right. Lesson 3 lets it fetch certificates.

choices.text: The Caddyfile syntax requires a scheme
choices.why: A bare domain is valid; it means HTTPS.

choices.text: To make the log JSON
choices.why: Caddy's log is JSON either way.

prompt: Which command is Caddy's equivalent of `nginx -t`?
hint: It printed `Valid configuration`.

choices.text: `caddy run`
choices.why: That starts a server.

choices.text: `caddy fmt`
choices.why: That reformats the file and tests nothing about it.

choices.text: `caddy validate`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `caddy reload --force`
choices.why: Reload applies a configuration; validate checks one without applying it.

prompt: The same `site.css` got three different `ETag`s from Nginx, Apache and Caddy. When does that become a problem?
hint: A client hands back the tag it was given.

choices.text: When the file grows larger than a megabyte
choices.why: Size changes nothing about which format each server uses.

choices.text: When a client asks for a gzip-compressed copy
choices.why: That changes the tag on one server; the formats differ anyway.

choices.text: When the browser runs JavaScript on the page
choices.why: ETags are an HTTP matter, not a scripting one.

choices.text: When two servers answer for one name
choices.why: Right. Every revalidation then downloads the whole file again.

prompt: Match each server to how it handles connections on the lab's machine.
hint: Look at NLWP.

pairs.right: single-threaded workers, each with an event loop
one process, goroutines over a few threads

prompt: A site has ten thousand mobile clients that each keep a connection open and send a request every few seconds. Which design pays least for the idle time?
hint: What does an idle connection occupy in each design?

choices.text: Apache prefork
choices.why: Ten thousand processes, one per connection.

choices.text: An event loop, as in Nginx's workers
choices.why: Right. An idle connection costs a few kilobytes and no thread.

choices.text: One thread per connection
choices.why: Ten thousand threads mostly waiting.

choices.text: Any of them, since the requests are small
choices.why: The cost here is the waiting, not the request.

prompt: The benchmark served site.css at between 11,853 and 19,176 requests a second. What is the lesson's conclusion?
hint: The ranking changed between runs.

choices.text: Nginx is the fastest and should always be chosen
choices.why: The ranking changed from one run to the next.

choices.text: Caddy is too slow for production
choices.why: Thousands a second for a static file is not slow.

choices.text: For a static file none of them is the bottleneck; choose on behaviour, configuration and who maintains it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: ab measured the network, which was slow
choices.why: There was no network: the same machine sent and served.

prompt: For the same request, Nginx logged 237 bytes and Apache logged 506. Why?
hint: Same column, two meanings.

choices.text: Apache compressed the file first
choices.why: Compression would make it smaller, not larger.

choices.text: It counted the headers too
choices.why: Right. Nginx counted the body only.

choices.text: The two files on disk are different
choices.why: Same file, same Content-Length of 237.

choices.text: ab sent a larger request to Apache
choices.why: The column is the response, not the request.

prompt: After `systemctl reload nginx`, which processes are new?
hint: Compare the PIDs before and after.

choices.text: All five
choices.why: The master kept PID 227.

choices.text: None
choices.why: The worker PIDs changed.

choices.text: Only the master
choices.why: The opposite: the master stayed.

choices.text: The workers; the master is the same process
choices.why: Right. Old workers finish their requests and exit.

prompt: With `rooot` typed in the server block, `systemctl reload` left the site answering 200 and `systemctl restart` left it answering 000. Why the difference?
hint: What runs while the new configuration is being checked?

choices.text: Restart ignores the error and reload notices it
choices.why: Both noticed the error; they differ in what was running when they did.

choices.text: One checks before touching the running server; the other stops it first
choices.why: Right. Test, then reload.

choices.text: Reload never reads the file, so the typo was never seen
choices.why: It read it and refused it.

choices.text: 000 is a cached copy of the page from before the change, not an outage
choices.why: 000 is curl saying nothing answered.

prompt: Put the safe way to apply a configuration change in order.
hint: The test comes before anything touches the running server.
trap: Reloading before testing is how a typo reaches the running server.

prompt: You add a second site, `static.ipelivros.example`, as a new server block on port 80. Nginx is running. Which sequence puts it online without refusing any request on the first site?
hint: Nothing in the sequence may stop the master.

choices.text: Link, `nginx -t`, reload
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Link it, then `systemctl restart nginx`
choices.why: A restart refuses connections in between, and a typo leaves both sites down.

choices.text: Start a second Nginx just for the new site
choices.why: Port 80 is taken; it would fail like Apache did.

choices.text: Put its files in `/var/www/html`
choices.why: That is the default site's root, not a new site with its own name.

prompt: A colleague's server answers `curl http://203.0.113.10/` with their admin panel's login page, although the panel is only meant to be reached as `admin.example.net`. What explains it?
hint: Which block answers a name nobody listed?

choices.text: The address is wrong in DNS
choices.why: No name was used at all; the request went to the address.

choices.text: The panel is the default server
choices.why: Right. Lesson 4 makes the default refuse instead.

choices.text: Nginx ignores server_name when given an IP address
choices.why: It uses server_name for every request; nothing matched, so the default answered.

choices.text: curl sent the request to the wrong port
choices.why: Port 80 is right; the name is the issue.

prompt: Which of these does `nginx -t` catch before a reload? Choose all that apply.
hint: It parses the configuration and checks what it can without serving.

choices.text: An unknown directive such as `rooot`
choices.why: Right. It printed `unknown directive`.

choices.text: A missing closing brace
choices.why: Right. The file does not parse.

choices.text: A page with a broken link in its HTML
choices.why: Nginx never reads the content it serves.

choices.text: A root directory that exists but holds the wrong site
choices.why: Valid configuration, wrong intention; no test can know that.
